Why Does My Dental Implant Feel Different When I Bite?

Written By

Dental Implants Team

Introduction

Many people who have received dental implants at some point notice that something feels slightly off when they bite down. Whether it is a subtle pressure difference, a sense of height, or an unusual sensation that was not present before, it is a common concern that prompts patients to search for answers online. Understanding why a dental implant can feel different when biting is an important part of knowing what to monitor and when to seek professional guidance.

Dental implants are designed to function much like natural teeth, but the way the body perceives bite force through an implant differs from a natural tooth root. This distinction is a key part of understanding any unusual sensations. In most cases, these feelings are perfectly explainable — but occasionally they may indicate something worth investigating further.

This article will explore the most common reasons a dental implant may feel different when you bite, including the underlying dental science, signs that may warrant a professional assessment, and practical advice to help you care for your implant long term.

A dental implant can feel different when biting because it lacks the periodontal ligament found around natural teeth, which normally cushions and senses bite pressure. Changes in bite sensation may also relate to implant crown height, the osseointegration process, or surrounding gum and bone changes. A dental professional can assess the cause accurately.

How a Dental Implant Differs From a Natural Tooth

To understand why bite sensation through a dental implant may feel unfamiliar, it helps to consider the anatomy involved. Natural teeth are not rigidly fixed directly into the jawbone. Instead, they are held in place by a structure called the periodontal ligament — a network of fine fibrous tissue that connects the tooth root to the surrounding bone.

This ligament does far more than simply anchor the tooth. It acts as a natural shock absorber during biting and chewing, distributing force evenly and providing the brain with detailed sensory feedback about pressure, texture, and bite load. This feedback mechanism is known as proprioception, and it is remarkably sensitive.

A dental implant, by contrast, is made from titanium and integrates directly into the jawbone through a process called osseointegration. While this creates an exceptionally stable and durable foundation, it does not replicate the periodontal ligament. As a result, the way biting force is transmitted and perceived through an implant is inherently different. Many patients describe their implant as feeling slightly "harder" or "more direct" when biting — and this is often simply a normal characteristic of how implants function. Understanding this can offer considerable reassurance when unusual sensations are first noticed.

Common Reasons Your Dental Implant May Feel Different When Biting

There are several reasons why a dental implant bite may feel unusual. Not all of these are causes for concern, but each is worth understanding clearly.

1. The Healing and Osseointegration Period

In the weeks and months following implant placement, the implant is still integrating with the surrounding bone. During this period, the bite may feel slightly different as the supporting tissues adapt. This is entirely expected and typically resolves as healing progresses.

2. Crown or Prosthetic Height

One of the most common reasons patients notice a change in bite sensation is a crown that sits slightly too high or too low relative to the opposing teeth. Even a fraction of a millimetre can be noticeable. If your bite feels uneven or you find yourself consistently hitting the implant crown first when closing your teeth together, this is worth discussing with your dental team as it can usually be corrected with a simple adjustment. You may also find this useful context on why an implant crown can feel too high even when it looks fine.

3. Changes in Adjacent Teeth

The natural teeth surrounding an implant can shift over time. If neighbouring teeth have moved, worn down, or been restored, this can alter how the bite falls across the implant, creating an unfamiliar sensation.

4. Loose Components

Dental implants typically consist of several components: the implant fixture, an abutment, and a crown. If the abutment screw becomes slightly loose, this can cause movement or a rocking sensation when biting. This is not something to ignore and should be assessed promptly.

5. Bone or Gum Changes Around the Implant

Over time, changes in the bone or gum tissue surrounding an implant — sometimes referred to as peri-implant changes — can affect how the implant sits and functions. These changes may be subtle initially but can affect long-term implant stability.

Understanding Peri-Implant Health and Its Role in Bite Sensation

Peri-implant health refers to the condition of the soft and hard tissues directly surrounding a dental implant. Just as gum disease can affect natural teeth and alter how they feel when biting, inflammation or tissue changes around an implant can have a similar effect.

Peri-implant mucositis is a reversible inflammatory condition affecting the gum tissue around an implant. It is comparable to gingivitis around natural teeth and, if detected early, can often be managed effectively with professional cleaning and improved home care.

Peri-implantitis is a more advanced condition involving inflammation and progressive bone loss around the implant. It shares similarities with periodontitis and, if left unmanaged, can compromise implant stability over time. Symptoms may include tenderness around the implant, bleeding when cleaning, and — relevant to this article — changes in how the implant feels when biting or applying pressure.

Maintaining excellent oral hygiene around implants is essential, and patients should attend regular professional reviews so that any early changes in peri-implant health can be identified and addressed appropriately. Signs That May Warrant a Professional Dental Assessment

Most changes in bite sensation following implant placement are minor and can be explained by the factors discussed above. However, certain symptoms are worth reporting to a dental professional promptly.

You may wish to arrange a dental assessment if you notice any of the following:

  • Persistent pain or discomfort when biting or chewing that does not settle within a few days
  • Swelling, redness, or tenderness in the gum tissue surrounding the implant
  • Bleeding around the implant when brushing or using interdental aids
  • Movement or rocking of the implant crown when pressure is applied
  • A noticeable change in the height of your bite that feels consistently uneven
  • A clicking or unusual sensation when teeth come together that was not previously present
  • Visible changes to the gum or bone around the implant site

None of these symptoms should cause undue alarm, but they do indicate that a professional assessment would be helpful. Early review allows any issue to be identified and addressed before it has the opportunity to progress. Dental symptoms and treatment options should always be assessed individually during a clinical examination.

What Happens During an Implant Assessment?

If you attend a dental practice with concerns about your implant bite sensation, the clinician will typically conduct a thorough assessment that may include:

  • Visual examination of the crown, gum tissue, and surrounding teeth
  • Bite analysis using thin articulating paper to identify exactly how and where your teeth are making contact
  • Radiographic (X-ray) review to assess the bone levels around the implant and the integrity of all components
  • Component checks to ensure the abutment and crown are securely fitted
  • Probing of the soft tissue around the implant to evaluate gum health

Based on the findings, the clinician may recommend a simple bite adjustment, professional cleaning, tightening or replacement of a loose component, or a more detailed treatment plan if peri-implant changes are identified. Treatment suitability always depends on individual clinical findings.

Caring for Your Dental Implant to Maintain a Comfortable Bite

Good ongoing care plays a significant role in implant longevity and comfortable function. While dental implants do not decay in the same way natural teeth do, the surrounding gum and bone tissue still require careful attention.

Practical care advice includes:

  • Brushing twice daily using a soft-bristled toothbrush, paying careful attention to the gum margin around the implant
  • Using interdental brushes or implant-specific floss to clean between and around the implant effectively — regular floss can sometimes be difficult to manoeuvre around implant components
  • Attending regular dental and hygiene appointments so that the implant, surrounding tissues, and overall bite can be monitored professionally
  • Avoiding habits that place excessive force on the implant, such as bruxism (tooth grinding) — if you grind at night, discuss this with your dentist as a night guard may be recommended
  • Avoiding very hard or sticky foods that may place undue stress on the crown or underlying components
  • Reporting any changes in sensation, comfort, or appearance to your dental team promptly rather than waiting for a routine appointment

For patients with multiple missing teeth or more complex restoration needs, understanding the range of implant-supported bridge options available may also be helpful when planning long-term oral health care.

Key Points to Remember

  • A dental implant can feel different when biting because it lacks the periodontal ligament of a natural tooth — this is a normal characteristic of implants
  • The most common reasons for bite changes include crown height adjustment needs, loose components, changes in adjacent teeth, or early peri-implant tissue changes
  • Not all unusual bite sensations are cause for concern, but persistent discomfort, movement, swelling, or bleeding around an implant warrants professional assessment
  • Regular dental reviews are essential for monitoring implant health and bite balance over time
  • Excellent oral hygiene around implants helps to maintain healthy peri-implant tissue and support long-term implant stability
  • Treatment and clinical advice should always be tailored to the individual following a proper examination

Frequently Asked Questions

Is it normal for a dental implant to feel different from a natural tooth?

Yes, it is entirely normal for a dental implant to feel somewhat different from a natural tooth. The primary reason is the absence of the periodontal ligament, which is the cushioning connective tissue that surrounds natural tooth roots. This ligament provides sensory feedback and shock absorption. Without it, the sensation of biting through an implant can feel more direct or slightly harder. Most patients adapt to this difference naturally over time, and it does not typically indicate a problem with the implant itself.

What does it mean if my dental implant feels high when I bite?

If your dental implant crown feels high — meaning you notice it making contact before your other teeth when you close your mouth — this is often a sign that a bite adjustment may be needed. Even a very slight difference in crown height is detectable because of how sensitive our bite perception is. This is a straightforward issue that a dental professional can assess and address, typically by carefully adjusting the crown surface. It is advisable to report this sensation rather than waiting, as a consistently high bite can place additional stress on the implant over time.

Can a dental implant become loose over time?

While dental implants are designed to be a stable, long-term solution, certain components can occasionally loosen over time. Most commonly, the abutment screw — the connection between the implant fixture and the crown — may become slightly loose, which can cause movement or an unusual sensation when biting. The implant fixture itself, once fully integrated into the jawbone, should remain stable. However, conditions such as peri-implantitis can compromise the surrounding bone over time and affect stability. Any perceived movement in an implant should be assessed by a dental professional promptly.

How long does it take to get used to the bite sensation of a dental implant?

The adjustment period varies from person to person. Many patients find that they adapt to the different bite sensation of a dental implant within a few weeks after the final crown is placed. During the initial healing phase following implant surgery, temporary restorations are often used, and the final bite is only fully established once the permanent crown is fitted. If bite discomfort or an unusual sensation persists for more than a few weeks after final crown placement, it is sensible to book an appointment for a bite assessment rather than simply waiting for the sensation to resolve on its own.

What is peri-implantitis and could it affect how my implant feels?

Peri-implantitis is a condition involving inflammation and progressive loss of the bone that supports a dental implant. It is similar in nature to periodontitis, which affects natural teeth. As the supporting bone changes, the way an implant transmits bite force can also be affected, potentially leading to changes in sensation when biting or chewing. Other signs may include tenderness, bleeding when brushing around the implant, or visible gum changes. Peri-implantitis is best addressed early, and regular professional monitoring plays an important role in detection. A dental professional will be able to assess the health of the tissues around your implant and advise on any appropriate steps.

Should I be concerned if my dental implant is sensitive to pressure?

A dental implant itself — being a titanium fixture — does not have nerve endings and cannot experience sensitivity in the way a natural tooth can. However, the surrounding gum tissue and bone do contain nerve supply, and pressure-related discomfort in the area around an implant is worth investigating. It could relate to gum inflammation, changes in peri-implant tissue, a loose component, or bite imbalance. In most cases, the cause is identifiable and manageable. If you are experiencing persistent pressure sensitivity around a dental implant, arranging a professional assessment is a sensible step.

Conclusion

Noticing that your dental implant feels different when you bite is a surprisingly common experience, and in many cases it can be explained by entirely normal physiological differences between implants and natural teeth. The absence of the periodontal ligament means that bite force is transmitted and sensed differently through an implant — something many patients become accustomed to over time.

That said, there are situations where changes in bite sensation may indicate that a professional review would be beneficial, whether to adjust the crown height, tighten a component, or assess the health of the surrounding tissues. Prompt attention to any persistent or concerning symptoms is always advisable.

Good oral hygiene, regular professional reviews, and open communication with your dental team remain the cornerstones of maintaining a healthy, comfortable dental implant long term. If you have noticed a change in how your implant feels when biting, or if you have any concerns about your implant, speaking with a qualified dental professional is an appropriate next step.

Dental symptoms and treatment options should always be assessed individually during a clinical examination.
